planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this is the wild-type variety that gave rise to the famous 'Goldsturm' selection, and it shows more natural variation in height and bloom timing than the uniform named cultivar.

directions: This straight variety of orange coneflower is the wild Ozark and southeastern-plains native from which the ubiquitous cultivar 'Goldsturm' was selected, so it shares the same rhizomatous, colony-forming habit and golden, dark-coned late-summer daisies but with more genetic variability in height and petal form plant to plant. It provides a long midsummer-to-fall nectar and pollen source for native bees, butterflies, and skippers, and the seed heads feed goldfinches through winter if left standing. Grow it where a slightly looser, more naturalistic look than the uniform cultivar is wanted, such as a pollinator meadow or informal cottage border, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Colrain Red Bee Balm (Top-Performing Mildew-Resistant Scarlet Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; give Colrain Red generous air circulation, which reinforces its already strong resistance to powdery mildew through humid summers.

directions: Colrain Red ranked among the top performers in Mt. Cuba Center's multi-year Monarda trial, prized for combining tall, vivid scarlet-red flower heads with foliage that stays notably clean of powdery mildew through a full humid growing season. The tubular blooms are a magnet for ruby-throated hummingbirds and are worked steadily by bumblebees and swallowtail butterflies from midsummer onward. Like other tall bee balms it spreads by shallow rhizomes into a broadening clump, so divide it every two to three years in early spring to keep the colony contained and airy. Best flower color and disease resistance come from siting it where morning sun is followed by light afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf South summers.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Trial Garden Report — Monarda

common_name: Bee-You Bee-True Bee Balm (Compact Raspberry-Red Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bee-True is a compact, mildew-resistant member of the Bee-You series bred for strong disease resistance in humid climates.

directions: Bee-True carries rich raspberry-red blooms centered on a contrasting brown button, a deeper, cooler-toned red than the vermillion of its Bee-Happy series-mate, on a dense, compact mound that stays well under two feet tall. Like the rest of the Bee-You series it was bred for strong resistance to powdery mildew, letting it hold clean foliage through a full Gulf South summer where older bee balm cultivars typically decline. Bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies visit its shaggy tubular flowers steadily through the midsummer bloom season. Provide good air circulation and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: AB Cultivars — US Plant Patent PP29079

common_name: Bee-You Bee-Lieve Bee Balm (Compact Pale Pink Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bee-Lieve is a compact, mildew-resistant member of the Bee-You series with an unusually soft pastel flower color for the genus.

directions: Bee-Lieve stands out in the Bee-You series for its true pale pink flowers, a softer pastel tone than the vivid reds and purples of most modern bee balm introductions, held on a dense, compact mound under two feet tall. It shares the series' strong resistance to powdery mildew, an important trait for keeping foliage attractive through a humid Gulf South summer. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit the shaggy tubular blooms through the midsummer season, and the soft color pairs easily with both hot and cool-toned companions in a pollinator border. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: AB Cultivars — US Plant Patent PP29078

common_name: Baby Cole Gaillardia (Dwarf Bicolor Blanket Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow seed on the soil surface (needs light to germinate, do not cover) or plant container divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Baby Cole needs excellent drainage even more than standard-size gaillardia because of its tighter, low crown.

directions: Baby Cole is one of the smallest named blanket flower selections, forming a dense mound only six to eight inches tall that still carries the classic three-inch, maroon-centered, red-and-yellow bicolor daisies of standard-size Gaillardia. Its diminutive scale makes it a natural fit for rock gardens, container edges, and the very front of a hot, dry border where a full-size blanket flower would sprawl out of proportion. It blooms from late spring through fall with only light deadheading, drawing bees and butterflies over an unusually long season for such a compact plant. Excellent drainage and lean soil are essential, since Baby Cole is even more prone to crown rot in heavy, humid-summer clay than its larger relatives.

common_name: Heat It Up Yellow Blanket Flower (Semi-Double Golden Interspecific Hybrid)
scientific_name: Gaillardia x grandiflora 'Heat It Up Yellow'

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Heat It Up Yellow was bred through interspecific crossing for improved disease resistance and does not require deadheading to rebloom.

directions: Heat It Up Yellow bears masses of semi-double, golden-yellow daisies with a darker gold eye continuously from late spring to mid fall without any deadheading, a real improvement over older seed-grown blanket flowers that need regular grooming to keep flowering. It won a Classic City Award from the University of Georgia trial gardens for its combination of heat tolerance and disease resistance bred into this interspecific hybrid line. Bees and butterflies visit the abundant blooms throughout the long season, and the flowers hold up well as cut flowers too. Give it lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since like all Gaillardia it declines quickly in rich, wet ground.
sources: University of Georgia Trial Gardens — Classic City Award

common_name: Torch Red Ember Blanket Flower (Fully Double Mahogany-Red Firewheel)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Torch Red Ember is grown as a warm-season annual and forms a neat, well-branched mound that needs no staking.

directions: Torch Red Ember is a Ball Horticultural selection from native Texas firewheel bred for fully double, two-inch mahogany-red pompom flowers on a tidy, low, spreading mound, a striking departure from the flat single blooms of wild Gaillardia pulchella. It flowers continuously from shortly after germination through summer heat into fall, holding up to Gulf South humidity with notably better mildew tolerance than many older annual gaillardia strains. Bees and butterflies work the abundant blooms all season, and deadheading is optional since the plant flowers heavily regardless. Direct sow into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun after frost danger passes, and expect reliable self-sowing in warm climates where the parent species is native.

common_name: Torch Yellow Blanket Flower (Fully Double Golden Firewheel)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Torch Yellow is the solid-gold sibling of the Torch series and forms the same neat, well-branched mound that needs no staking.

directions: Torch Yellow is the golden-flowered member of the Ball Horticultural Torch series bred from native Texas firewheel, producing fully double, two-inch, solid-yellow pompom flowers on the same low, well-branched, self-supporting mound as its Torch Red Ember series-mate. It blooms continuously from shortly after germination through the heat of summer into fall, tolerating Gulf Coast humidity with better mildew resistance than many older seed-grown gaillardia strains. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers heavily throughout the long season, and the fully double blooms hold up well in cut arrangements. Direct sow into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun after frost danger passes and expect the plant to self-sow readily in warm climates.

common_name: Presto Coreopsis (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Dwarf Double Tickseed)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Presto flowers heavily from seed its first year on a compact, well-branched plant.

directions: Presto won a Fleuroselect Gold Medal for producing unusually large, semi-double to double, golden-yellow flowers on a dwarf, tidy plant that stays well under fifteen inches tall, making it a more compact alternative to older tall tickseed strains. It flowers heavily from seed within its first season and continues through summer with light deadheading, drawing bees, small butterflies, and other pollinators to its abundant blooms. Its short, well-branched habit resists flopping without staking, unlike many taller Coreopsis grandiflora selections. Give it lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since excellent drainage is essential to prevent crown rot in humid Gulf South summers.
